entities.summary:
The 1918–1920 global influenza pandemic, caused by the H1N1 influenza A virus, was a catastrophic event that ravaged the world, claiming millions of lives and reshaping the course of human history.

This pandemic, which occurred during a time of unprecedented global turmoil, was sparked by the Spanish Flu's rapid spread across the globe, infecting an estimated 500 million people and killing between 50 and 100 million, making it one of the deadliest natural disasters in human history.

The pandemic had a profound impact on global society, leading to widespread lockdowns, border closures, and a profound shift in the way people lived, worked, and interacted with one another. It also accelerated the development of modern medicine, including the creation of vaccines and diagnostic tools, and had a lasting impact on the world's public health infrastructure.

The 1918–1920 flu pandemic serves as a stark reminder of the fragility of human societies and the devastating consequences of a global health crisis. Its legacy continues to shape our understanding of the interconnectedness of the world and the need for global cooperation in the face of emerging health threats.

A staggering 50 million deaths worldwide, and a global economic downturn, the 1918-1920 flu pandemic had a lasting impact on the world, and continues to be studied by historians and scholars today.
